extracted.intended_audience: scientists and educated general readers (Popular Science Monthly audience) interested in physiology/psychology and social theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and observational standards for assessing experimental reports on hypnotism (and, secondarily, guidance for interpreting objections about the theory of evolution in social/biological contexts). Focuses on stages, memory, sensory/motor changes, induction/awakening methods, and aggregate-level interpretation of evolutionary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of hypnotism and memory retention
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypnotic condition occurs in distinct stages: in the first (least profound) stage the patient, on being awakened, can remember all that happened; in the second (more profound) stage the patient can only partially recollect; in the third (most profound) stage all power of subsequent recollection is lost, although sensory perception remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when memory is absent on awakening, it may be aroused by giving the patient a clew (e.g., a single word or a line of poetry). Compare these stages to varying depths of reverie where recall may sometimes be achieved by effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic performance of habitual actions (motor mimicry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions rendered 'mechanical' by frequent repetition are performed automatically in hypnosis; there is a strong tendency to imitate the operator's movements (e.g., opening/closing a hand) and to follow movements or sounds that stand in customary relation to those actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To constitute stimuli for automatic movements, the sounds or gestures must have a customary relation to the movements they suggest; imitation can occur from sight or even from sound alone (operator-visible hand movement or clattering of teeth). This criterion is relevant when judging reported motor responses and experimental controls for suggestion/imitative cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaltation of sensibility to slight stimuli and diminished response to strong stimuli
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypnotic state often shows extraordinary exaltation of sensibility so that very slight stimuli (ineffective normally) are effective, while excitability toward strong stimuli is greatly diminished (deeply hypnotized persons may show no signs of discomfort when cut or burned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the remarkable similarity to certain pathological derangements of the central nervous system and to stages of anaesthesia where contact is felt but pain is not. Reports should document both increased sensitivity to weak stimuli and decreased responsiveness to strong/painful stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased reflex excitability, irradiation, and slow propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflex sensibility increases in hypnotism; gentle stimulation may cause contraction only of adjacent muscles and, with increasing stimulus strength, excitation spreads progressively to further muscle groups (following Pfluger's law of irradiation). Propagation of reflex excitation through central organs is slower than in ordinary conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect muscles to be prone to tonic contraction (cramp/catalepsy) and for reflex changes to persist for days in some cases (e.g., inability to straighten an arm for several days after induced flexion). Reports should measure duration and spatial spread of reflex effects and compare propagation rates to normal baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency toward tonic contraction and catalepsy-like rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypnotic condition strongly resembles catalepsy: muscles may go into tonic contraction making the body rigid (e.g., supporting a person's head and feet only may allow someone to stand on the stomach without yielding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental observations should note degree and duration of tonic contraction, susceptibility differences among subjects, and any functional consequences (immobility, posture retention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological signs (respiration and pulse changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heidenhain observed increases in rate of breathing (up to fourfold) and an acceleration of pulse, though less pronounced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports should include objective physiological measurements (respiratory rate, pulse, etc.) to document systemic effects and help distinguish hypnotic state from other altered states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction conditions for hypnotism
rubrics_metrics.description: No special 'force' is required; susceptibility varies (greatest in persons of high nervous sensibility). Hypnotic state may be induced by gentle, continuous, monotonous sensory stimuli of touch, sight, or hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical induction methods include continuous staring at a small bright object, listening to a monotonous sound, or being gently and continuously stroked on the skin. Experimental protocols should specify stimulus modality, intensity, continuity, and subject susceptibility characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awakening / termination triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypnotic state may be terminated by a strong or sudden change in stimulation—examples include gently blowing upon the face, slapping the hand, screaming in the ear, or a change in retinal stimulus when another person suddenly takes the operator's place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports and protocols should define and control awakening stimuli; note that abrupt changes in sensory input are effective terminators, which has implications for safety and for interpreting spontaneous recovery of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity to pathological states and anaesthesia (interpretative criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypnotic condition shows interesting similarity or possible identity with certain pathological central nervous system derangements and with stages of anaesthesia (e.g., contact felt but pain absent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating hypnotism findings, compare features with known pathological and anaesthetic phenomena to avoid misattribution; this helps frame hypotheses about underlying mechanisms and clinical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive formulation of evolution (requirement for correct critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's formula: 'Evolution is an integration of matter and concomitant dissipation of motion; during which the matter passes from an indefinite, incoherent homogeneity to a definite, coherent heterogeneity; and during which the retained motion undergoes a parallel transformation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms of the evolutionary formula must consider all associated traits simultaneously; separating traits (e.g., homogeneity→heterogeneity vs integration/dissipation) may lead to misinterpretation of the formula's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate-level vs single-system analysis (interpretive caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish evolution of a single system (e.g., one language) from evolution of an aggregate (e.g., all languages); disappearance of dialects is extinction of varieties, not progress toward homogeneity within the surviving variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims about homogeneity/heterogeneity, clarify whether analysis refers to individual systems or aggregates. Failure to do so can cause erroneous conclusions (e.g., conflating integration with homogeneity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration can increase heterogeneity in parts (socioeconomic example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration (e.g., formation of joint-stock companies or large stores) is the primary evolutionary process and may be accompanied by greater heterogeneity — the aggregate of industrial structures becomes more varied because new forms are added rather than replacing all old forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate organizational/social changes by examining whether integration adds new differentiated parts (increasing overall heterogeneity) versus replacing old types (which could decrease heterogeneity); avoid equating amalgamation with despecialization without checking internal complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution is conditional and contingent on ongoing forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of evolution is not necessary or intrinsic but depends on prevailing conditions; progression toward more heterogeneous and definite structures continues only while the actions producing these effects continue; cessation of those actions halts the progression and may lead to dissolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret evolutionary transformations as contingent; when reviewing evolutionary claims, examine the sustaining conditions and whether they are present or have ceased (expect mixtures and transitory anomalies during metamorphoses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing evolutionary claims at appropriate scope (law of aggregates)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of evolution is a law of transformation of aggregates and must be tested by considering the entire assemblage of phenomena the aggregates present; isolated orders of social processes may show exceptions without falsifying the aggregate-level law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques or empirical tests should use whole-aggregate data (e.g., the structures and functions of an entire society or the totality of societies) rather than selective phenomena to judge the general law's applicability.
